title: The last arrow
hookLine: Agastya's hymn to the sun; Rama bows to Surya; Ravana falls
carry: surya: the sun greeted as divine light
last: SIX INNER ENEMIES, AND THEY GROW BACK.

lines: A SAGE WALKS ONTO THE FIELD.
cards: Near the end of something long, the last week of a hard job, the last exam, it gets hard to tell whether you're winning at all. The fight between Rama and Ravana has gone on and on.
The gods have sent Rama a chariot, Indra's own, driven by Indra's charioteer, Matali. Ravana's heads keep growing back. And Rama, in Valmiki's telling, is worn out, and worried.
Then an old sage walks onto the battlefield: Agastya. Instead of a weapon, he gives Rama words.

teach.b: Agastya teaches Rama a hymn to the sun, the Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun. Praise the sun, the sage tells him, the one who lights every world and wakes every living thing.
Recite this, and worry and grief will ease. So, in the middle of a war, Rama stops. He looks at the sun and recites the hymn, and in the story, strength comes back into him.
Devotees still chant it, some at sunrise, some before a hard day: the words a tired prince heard on a battlefield. Then Matali, the charioteer, speaks up. Remember the weapon made by Brahma, he says.
The time has come. Rama takes out an arrow given to him long before: the brahmastra, the weapon of the creator himself. He sets it to the bow and releases it.
It strikes Ravana in the chest, in the heart, and the king of Lanka falls from his chariot. The gods rain flowers. The war is over.
Later tellings add nectar hidden in Ravana's navel; in Valmiki, the weapon itself does the work. Rama, whom Hindus worship as God come to earth, still stops and bows to the sun before the end.

Many Hindus still greet the morning sun, Surya, palms joined, or pouring water from cupped hands toward it, with words like Om Suryaya Namah: I bow to the sun. The light that wakes every living thing, greeted as divine.
Before the phone, before the news, a moment turned toward the light. And every autumn, many Hindus celebrate Rama's victory at Dussehra, the victorious tenth day.

how: Devotees chant the Aditya Hridayam, the hymn Agastya teaches Rama, at sunrise or before difficult undertakings; Ravana's defeat is celebrated at Dussehra (Vijayadashami), when effigies of Ravana are burned in many towns.

o: a hymn to the sun that Agastya taught Rama in battle
a lullaby Sita sang to her sons in the forest
a prayer Ravana chanted to Shiva before he fell

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: taught Rama a hymn to the sun
water offered to the rising sun

s: the nectar in Ravana's navel is in Valmiki's Ramayana
it's from later tellings. in Valmiki, the brahmastra strikes Ravana in the chest.
people still chant the hymn Agastya taught Rama
the Aditya Hridayam is chanted today, often at sunrise or before hard days.
Rama won by fighting harder and faster
the turn comes after he stops in the middle of the war and prays to the sun.

games.q: a friend asks why her grandmother pours water toward the sun every morning. what fits today's teaching?
o: she's greeting Surya, the sun, as divine light; even Rama bowed to the sun before his last battle.
she's watering the plants on the balcony.
it's just for luck. it doesn't mean anything.
games.why: offering water to the rising sun, arghya, is a daily Hindu practice. the Aditya Hridayam is one of the hymns said to the sun.

practice: If you can see daylight, turn toward it; if not, face where the sun would be. Join your palms, or cup your hands as if holding water to pour toward it, and say quietly: Om Suryaya Namah, I bow to the sun.
If you don't pray, just let the light reach your face and think of one hard thing in front of you this week. Rama stopped in the middle of a war to do this.

wordCard.voice: Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun: the hymn Agastya gives a tired Rama before the last arrow.

orig.note: Sanskrit: aditya (the sun) + hridayam (heart). 'The heart of the sun', Agastya's hymn.

carryVoice: Your line: Surya, the sun greeted as divine light. Even Rama stopped for it. Day sixty-six, and the war is done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (the closing duel: Agastya's Aditya Hridayam; Matali's counsel; the brahmastra; Ravana's death)
Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand (the nectar in Ravana's navel)
greeting the rising sun: arghya (water offering) and the name-mantra Om Suryaya Namah
Dussehra (Vijayadashami) kept as the day of Rama's victory over Ravana
